source: MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture, banana cultivation techniques manual, 2019, section V.2.2 (pseudostem weevil)
text:
The banana pseudostem weevil (Odoiporus longicollis, cited in the source as Odoiporus longicoollis) is a blackish beetle roughly 3.5cm long with orange-tinged markings and the elongated snout typical of weevils. Unlike the corm weevil, this species bores through the pseudostem (trunk) itself rather than the underground corm. Adults lay eggs in wounds or cuts on the stem; larvae tunnel extensively through the leaf-sheath layers that make up the pseudostem, weakening its structure — particularly dangerous near the growing crown, where damage can cause stunted growth or cause the whole plant to snap or collapse, especially once it is carrying a heavy bunch.

External tunneling holes, often oozing sap or frass, are visible signs of infestation. The full life cycle from egg to adult takes roughly a month.

Prevention and control: keep the field clear of dry stem debris and old plant material that shelters the weevil; avoid overly wet soil conditions; plan crop rotation where infestations are severe; disinfect tools between plants; and where chemical control is warranted, granular insecticide can be worked into the planting hole/soil around the base before planting, mixed at the concentration recommended on the product label.
